_comment: IRC 125(i) health flexible spending arrangement and IRC 129 dependent care assistance dollar amounts taken verbatim from the annual IRS inflation-adjustment revenue procedures, the named notices, and the statutes in sources/. Verified 2026-08-30. Amounts are dollars. See README.md for method.

_sources.usc-26-125: 26 U.S.C. s.125 (U.S. Government Publishing Office, 2024 edition of the United States Code); s.125(i)(1)-(2) carry the $2,500 base amount and the indexing formula
_sources.usc-26-129: 26 U.S.C. s.129 (U.S. Government Publishing Office, 2024 edition of the United States Code); s.129(a)(2)(A) carries $5,000 ($2,500), s.129(a)(2)(D) the 2021 rule, s.129(b) the earned income limitation
_sources.usc-26-21: 26 U.S.C. s.21 (U.S. Government Publishing Office, 2024 edition of the United States Code); s.129(a)(2)(C) determines marital status under s.21(e)(3) and (4), and s.21(e)(4) is the considered-unmarried rule for a married individual filing separately who maintained a qualifying individual's principal place of abode for more than half the year, furnished over half its cost, and whose spouse was not a member of the household during the last six months. s.21(d)(2), the deemed earned income schedule, is present in this document but deliberately not encoded

_dependentCareComment: The IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amounts are not inflation adjusted, so no annual revenue procedure states them and they are cited to the Code and to the acts that changed them, the same way the HSA corpus cites the IRC 223(b)(3)(B) age-55 amount to the statute. The series starts at 1987 because Pub. L. 99-514 section 1163(a) added the limitation of exclusion applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986; before that IRC 129(a) carried no dollar cap, which the 1986 amendment note in usc-26-129 shows by quoting the prior text. The 1988 amendment note quotes the pre-1988 text of paragraph (2) with the same $5,000 ($2,500) figures, so the amounts ran unbroken from 1987 to 2020 and again from 2022 to 2025.
_healthFsaCarryoverComment: The carryover is an IRS-created plan option, not a statutory one, and it belongs to the plan year the amounts are carried FROM. Notice 2013-71 created it at a fixed $500; Notice 2020-33 raised it to 20 percent of the IRC 125(i) limit for that plan year. Rev. Proc. 2013-35 through Rev. Proc. 2019-44 state the IRC 125(i) limit and no carryover figure, so 2013 through 2019 are cited to Notice 2013-71 and 2020 to Notice 2020-33. Rev. Proc. 2020-45 is the first annual procedure here to state a carryover amount itself.

L. 99-514 section 1163(a) amended IRC 129(a) generally to add the limitation of exclusion, applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986 (section 1163(c)). See usc-26-129, whose 1988 amendment note quotes the pre-1988 text of paragraph (2) with the same $5,000 ($2,500) figures.

2018.healthFsaSalaryReductionLimit_125i_sourc: Rev. Proc. 2017-58 section 3.16 (Cafeteria Plans). Rev. Proc. 2018-18 (irb18-10) reissued the 2018 figures after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act changed the indexing measure, but its sections 3 and 5 list the modified and superseded sections of Rev. Proc. 2017-58 as running 3.14, 3.15, 3.18 - section 3.16 is absent - so the Cafeteria Plans figure was neither restated nor changed.

2020.healthFsaCarryoverLimit_source: Notice 2020-33 section III.A raised the carryover to 20 percent of the IRC 125(i) limit for that plan year and states $550 for a plan year starting in 2020 (20 percent of $2,750). Rev. Proc. 2019-44 states no carryover figure.

2021.healthFsaCarryoverLimit_source: Rev. Proc. section stated above, "If the cafeteria plan permits the carryover of unused amounts, the maximum carryover amount is $550" for taxable years beginning in 2021; the 20-percent rule itself is Notice 2020-33 (20 percent of $2750).
2021.dependentCareExclusion_129a2A_source: American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, Pub. L. 117-2, section 9632(a), adding IRC 129(a)(2)(D): for a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2022, subparagraph (A) is applied by substituting "$10,500 (half such dollar amount" for "$5,000 ($2,500". Half of $10,500 is $5,250. Section 9632(b) applies the amendment to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2020. This is not an inflation adjustment, so no revenue procedure carries it; Rev. Proc. 2020-45 predates the March 2021 enactment and could not.

2026.dependentCareExclusion_129a2A_source: Pub. L. 119-21, section 70404(a), striking "$5,000 ($2,500" from IRC 129(a)(2)(A) and inserting "$7,500 ($3,750"; section 70404(b) applies the amendment to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. A fixed-dollar substitution with no indexing mechanism, so no revenue procedure carries it. usc-26-129 is the 2024 edition of the Code and still prints $5,000/$2,500.
